headline: Parliament Passes Climate Liability Bill and Advances Disability Services Framework Amid Cost-of-Living Disputes
summary: Parliament passed a law barring climate-related emissions liability claims in tort, while advancing a new disability support framework despite opposition concerns about rights, family care and scrutiny. MPs also questioned the Government over winter energy payments mistakenly withheld from about 15,000 pensioners and veterans, and clashed over grocery prices and the removal of Chris Penk as a Minister. The House unanimously passed legislation transferring legal title to Nelson Tenths land to its trust.

topicSummaries.topic: About 15,000 Pensioners and Veterans Miss Winter Energy Payments
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The payment error temporarily reduced help with energy bills for older people and veterans during winter, although the Government said affected payments were corrected.
topicSummaries.content: The Prime Minister said it was unacceptable that about 14,800 pensioners and veterans had missed winter energy payments, and apologised. Social Development Minister Louise Upston said a policy omission was carried through the legislative and IT processes; she said the maximum amount affected was less than $300 per person, all affected payments had been corrected within 48 hours of her learning of the issue, and a review was under way. Labour questioned whether rushed lawmaking contributed to the error. Ricardo Menéndez March’s request for an urgent debate on the payment issue was declined because the Speaker gave priority to a debate on Chris Penk’s removal as a Minister.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Will she admit that rushing legislation through Parliament without proper scrutiny meant that her mistake left vulnerable people without heating in a freezing cold winter?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: No. As I’ve said, the omission occurred in the policy development, and of course it is very unfortunate that this has occurred, which is why I asked MSD, with urgency, to fix it to ensure that people did not go without.

topicSummaries.topic: Food Inflation Falls to 1.9% as MPs Dispute Supermarket Pricing
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Food and rent are major household costs, and the debate highlighted the difference between slower price increases and lower prices for consumers.
topicSummaries.content: The Government cited annual food price inflation of 1.9 percent in the year to July, down from the much higher rates recorded in 2022 and 2023. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon argued that inflation was easing and said the Government was pursuing more grocery-sector competition, including by making it easier to build supermarket infrastructure. Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick pressed him on Commerce Commission findings of excess supermarket profits and called for a prohibition on excessive pricing; Luxon did not endorse that proposal. Housing Minister Chris Bishop also reported annual rent growth of 0.1 percent in July, the lowest in almost 25 years, and said rents had become more affordable.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does the Prime Minister disagree, then, with the Commerce Commission, who have found that the supermarket duopoly are making excess profits of hundreds of millions of dollars, increasing the cost of living for New Zealanders?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, I think the member will also be very excited to hear that food price inflation has further come down to 1.9 percent—that’s good news. We also want to see more competition in the grocery sector; that would put more downward pressure into grocery prices as well, and that’s why we have a number of actions under way to do that.

topicSummaries.topic: Disability Support Services Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill creates a statutory framework for disability supports, but its rules could influence how services are delivered and how disabled people and their families receive assistance.
topicSummaries.content: The Disability Support Services Bill passed its second reading on the votes of National, ACT and New Zealand First; Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed it. Disability Issues Minister Louise Upston said it would clarify the system without changing current eligibility, entitlements or support, and pointed to amendments following almost 3,000 written submissions and about 140 oral submissions. Changes include more person-centred decision-making principles, consultation with representative groups on support programmes, a five-year transition period and a review of the Act within five years. Opponents argued the process was rushed and that the bill leaves important settings to secondary legislation, does not sufficiently guarantee that family care will complement rather than replace funded support, and limits some routes for legal claims. Further legislation on safeguarding, information gathering, appeals and complaints is planned.

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The bill does not result in any changes to current eligibility, entitlements, or support.

keyExchanges.speaker: Priyanca Radhakrishnan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The amended bill does not prohibit extending means testing beyond its present use.

topicSummaries.topic: Climate Liability Bill Passes Third Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law removes the possibility of emissions-related tort claims against businesses, including an existing case, changing how climate-related disputes can be pursued through the courts.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill at its third reading, with National, ACT and New Zealand First supporting it and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposing it. The law bars tort liability for emissions-related climate effects and applies to existing proceedings, including the case brought by Mike Smith against Fonterra and other major emitters. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the measure would keep climate policy-making with Parliament and the executive, avoid a parallel legal regime and provide certainty for businesses; he said it does not change national climate targets or businesses’ obligations under the emissions trading scheme. Opponents said it retrospectively cuts off access to the courts and prevents the case from being decided. Labour and Green speakers also criticised the bill’s development and raised concerns about lobbying and the shortened select committee process. Labour and the Greens said they would repeal it if elected.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The question is: should Parliament do that? I would say that Parliament should not do that, because it is an affront to our certainty of law—the fact that you would put in place retrospective legislation that would change the law.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government’s view is that tort law is not an appropriate mechanism for responding to greenhouse gas emissions.

topicSummaries.topic: Nelson Tenths Bill Transfers Legal Title to Te Here ā Nuku Trust
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The legislation gives the descendants of customary owners legal title to land held by the Crown for their benefit, while setting arrangements for public access and ongoing uses.
topicSummaries.content: The House unanimously passed the Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill at its third reading, following a negotiated resolution of a dispute rooted in promises made in the 19th century. Attorney-General Chris Bishop said the bill transfers legal title to trust land from the Crown to the trustees of Te Here ā Nuku Trust and gives effect to aspects of the agreement reached after litigation. New Zealand First MP David Wilson said the bill formally recognises approximately 3,250 hectares held in trust for descendants of the original customary owners. The legislation also provides for continuing conservation, reserve, education and other public uses; speakers said public access to Abel Tasman National Park, including the Coast Track and Tōtaranui campsite, would continue under agreed arrangements.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This case and its resolution and its settlement represents Parliament at its best, unanimously coming together to vindicate property rights and the rule of law.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Boyack (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The passage of this bill cannot undo the losses of the past, but it represents an important step toward making things right.

topicSummaries.topic: Opposition Challenges Luxon Over Chris Penk’s Removal
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute over the Prime Minister’s leadership and the dismissal of a senior Minister exposed divisions in the governing party while MPs argued that political infighting distracted from household pressures.
topicSummaries.content: The Speaker granted an urgent debate sought by Labour leader Chris Hipkins on Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s decision to remove Chris Penk as a Minister after Penk challenged his leadership. Hipkins questioned the Government’s account that Penk acted alone and accused National MPs of focusing on leadership tensions rather than cost-of-living pressures. National Minister Simeon Brown said Penk’s actions had made his Cabinet position untenable and that his portfolios had been reassigned. Green and Te Pāti Māori speakers also criticised the Government’s response to other ministerial conduct. The debate ended without a vote after the motion to take note of the matter lapsed.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The real question for New Zealanders is a pretty simple one: if Christopher Luxon’s own MPs don’t want him to be the leader of the National Party and the Prime Minister of New Zealand, why should New Zealanders think any differently?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The actions of Chris Penk ultimately made his position in Cabinet untenable, and, as such, he was removed from his portfolios, and they have been reallocated to other Ministers.

topicSummaries.topic: Pharmac Expands Access to Three Type 2 Diabetes Medicines
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Wider access to funded medicines can affect treatment options for people with diabetes and other conditions.
topicSummaries.content: Associate Health Minister David Seymour said Pharmac would widen access to three medicines for people with type 2 diabetes from 1 September, with eligibility based on clinical need rather than ancestry. He said Pharmac was reviewing ethnicity-based access criteria and described the change as part of the Government’s policy direction. Seymour also said the Government had allocated more than $7.2 billion to Pharmac over four years and that 135 decisions had funded medicines or widened access, including 47 cancer medicines. Labour MP Willie Jackson interrupted the exchange to dispute Seymour’s account of Pharmac’s changes.

keyExchanges.speaker: David Seymour (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Never again should two patients go to see their doctor with the exact same clinical need and be treated differently because of who their ancestors were.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Oh rubbish—what a load of rubbish.

topicSummaries.topic: Youth Justice Bill Committee Debate Continues
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed young serious offender declarations could affect court oversight, privacy and the duration of restrictions placed on young people.
topicSummaries.content: The House continued its committee-stage consideration of the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill, but did not complete the debate. Opposition MPs raised concerns about labelling young people, privacy, time limits, disability and mental health considerations, and the involvement of whānau and iwi. The Minister for Children, Karen Chhour, rejected several proposed amendments, saying existing Oranga Tamariki principles apply and that the two-year declaration period was needed to support meaningful change. The committee reported progress, with further consideration still required.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Given the significant impacts of such a declaration on a young person, a shorter default period, we argue, would be better and would better reflect the principles that interventions should be proportionate and no more restrictive than necessary.

keyExchanges.speaker: Karen Chhour (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I consider the two-year declaration length is necessary to make meaningful change in these young people’s lives.

conclusion: The day produced cross-party agreement on the Nelson Tenths settlement but sharp divisions over the Government’s approach to disability support, climate-related court claims and the cost pressures facing households.
